questions.text:
If '\(\rightarrow\)' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [dry \(\rightarrow\) arid \(\rightarrow\) parched] is analogous to [diet \(\rightarrow\) fast \(\rightarrow\) ________ ].
Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Dry, arid and parched are increasing degrees of lack of water. Likewise diet, fast and starve are increasing degrees of not eating: dieting cuts food, fasting stops it for a while, starving is going without food to an extreme. Feast is the opposite, and reject and deny are not about eating. Answer: starve.

questions.text: If two distinct non-zero real variables \(x\) and \(y\) are such that \((x+y)\) is proportional to \((x-y)\) then the value of \(\frac{x}{y}\)

options.label: B
options.text: depends only on \(x\) and not on \(y\)

options.label: C
options.text: depends only on \(y\) and not on \(x\)

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Write \(x+y = k(x-y)\) for a constant \(k\). Then \(x(1-k) = -y(1+k)\), so \(\frac{x}{y} = \frac{k+1}{k-1}\), which is a constant (it depends only on \(k\), not on \(x\) or \(y\)).

questions.text:
Consider the following sample of numbers:
9, 18, 11, 14, 15, 17, 10, 69, 11, 13
The median of the sample is
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Sorted: 9, 10, 11, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 69. There are 10 numbers, so the median is the mean of the 5th and 6th: \(\frac{13+14}{2} = 13.5\).

questions.text: The number of coins of ₹1, ₹5, and ₹10 denominations that a person has are in the ratio 5:3:13. Of the total amount, the percentage of money in ₹5 coins is
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Take 5, 3 and 13 coins. Money: ₹1 coins give 5, ₹5 coins give \(3 \times 5 = 15\), ₹10 coins give \(13 \times 10 = 130\). Total = 150. Share in ₹5 coins = \(\frac{15}{150} = 10\%\).

questions.text:
For positive non-zero real variables \(p\) and \(q\), if
\[\log\left(p^2+q^2\right) = \log p + \log q + 2\log 3,\]
then, the value of \(\frac{p^4+q^4}{p^2q^2}\) is
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: The right side is \(\log(9pq)\), so \(p^2+q^2 = 9pq\). Squaring: \(p^4 + 2p^2q^2 + q^4 = 81p^2q^2\), so \(p^4+q^4 = 79p^2q^2\). Hence \(\frac{p^4+q^4}{p^2q^2} = 79\).

questions.text:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)\(-\)(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
Steve was advised to keep his head ______ (i) before heading ______ (ii) to bat; for, while he had a head ______ (iii) batting, he could only do so with a cool head ______ (iv) his shoulders.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Keep one's head down = stay focused and out of trouble. A batter heads out to bat. Having a head for something = a natural talent for it. A cool head on one's shoulders = calm and sensible. So down, out, for, on.

questions.text:
A rectangular paper sheet of dimensions 54 cm \(\times\) 4 cm is taken. The two longer edges of the sheet are joined together to create a cylindrical tube. A cube whose surface area is equal to the area of the sheet is also taken.
Then, the ratio of the volume of the cylindrical tube to the volume of the cube is
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Joining the two 54 cm edges makes a tube of length 54 cm whose circumference is 4 cm, so \(r = \frac{2}{\pi}\). Volume of tube = \(\pi r^2 h = \pi \cdot \frac{4}{\pi^2} \cdot 54 = \frac{216}{\pi}\).
Sheet area = \(54 \times 4 = 216 = 6a^2\), so the cube's side is \(a = 6\) and its volume is 216.
Ratio = \(\frac{216/\pi}{216} = \frac{1}{\pi}\).

questions.text:
The pie chart presents the percentage contribution of different macronutrients to a typical 2,000 kcal diet of a person.
The typical energy density (kcal/g) of these macronutrients is given in the table.

| Macronutrient | Energy density (kcal/g) |
|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | 4 |
| Proteins | 4 |
| Unsaturated fat | 9 |
| Saturated fat | 9 |
| Trans fat | 9 |

The total fat (all three types), in grams, this person consumes is
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: From the pie chart, fats give 20% (unsaturated) + 20% (saturated) + 5% (trans) = 45% of 2,000 kcal = 900 kcal. All fats give 9 kcal/g, so the fat eaten is \(\frac{900}{9} = 100\) g.

questions.text: A rectangular paper of 20 cm \(\times\) 8 cm is folded 3 times. Each fold is made along the line of symmetry, which is perpendicular to its long edge. The perimeter of the final folded sheet (in cm) is
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Each fold halves the current long edge.
Fold 1: 20 \(\times\) 8 becomes 10 \(\times\) 8 (long edge 10).
Fold 2: 10 \(\times\) 8 becomes 5 \(\times\) 8 (now the long edge is 8).
Fold 3: fold perpendicular to the 8 cm edge, giving 5 \(\times\) 4.
Perimeter = \(2(5+4) = 18\) cm.

questions.text: The least number of squares to be added in the figure to make AB a line of symmetry is
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Mirror every square in the line AB and count the squares that are missing.

Left shape: one square above AB in its right column; below AB, two squares side by side and one more under the right one. Its mirror image needs, above AB, a second square beside the one already there and a square above that one. That is 2 squares.

Right shape: below AB, two squares side by side and one more under the right one; nothing above. Its mirror image needs two squares side by side above AB and one more above the right one. That is 3 squares.

In all, 2 + 3 = 5 squares.
questions.defect: IISc's final key marks 6 (option A), but the figure as printed needs 5 squares (option C), counted below.

questions.text: Let \(f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be a function such that \(f(x) = \max\{x, x^3\}\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), where \(\mathbb{R}\) is the set of all real numbers. The set of all points where \(f(x)\) is NOT differentiable is
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
\(x^3 - x = x(x-1)(x+1)\), so \(x^3 \geq x\) on \([-1, 0]\) and \([1, \infty)\), and \(x \geq x^3\) elsewhere. So \(f\) switches between \(x\) and \(x^3\) at \(x = -1, 0, 1\).
At each switch point the slopes differ: at \(x = \pm 1\), slope of \(x\) is 1 and of \(x^3\) is 3; at \(x = 0\), slope of \(x\) is 1 and of \(x^3\) is 0. So \(f\) has a corner at \(-1, 0, 1\) and is smooth elsewhere.

questions.text: The product of all eigenvalues of the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\) is
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: The product of the eigenvalues equals the determinant. Row 3 minus row 2 = (3, 3, 3) = row 2 minus row 1, so the rows are linearly dependent and the determinant is 0.

questions.text: Consider a system that uses 5 bits for representing signed integers in 2's complement format. In this system, two integers \(A\) and \(B\) are represented as \(A = 01010\) and \(B = 11010\). Which one of the following operations will result in either an arithmetic overflow or an arithmetic underflow?
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
5-bit 2's complement covers \(-16\) to \(+15\). \(A = 01010 = 10\), \(B = 11010 = -6\).
(A) \(A + B = 4\): fits.
(B) \(A - B = 16\): exceeds 15, overflow.
(C) \(B - A = -16\): fits (smallest value).
(D) \(2B = -12\): fits.
Only \(A - B\) overflows.

questions.text: Consider a permutation sampled uniformly at random from the set of all permutations of \(\{1, 2, 3, \cdots, n\}\) for some \(n \geq 4\). Let \(X\) be the event that 1 occurs before 2 in the permutation, and \(Y\) the event that 3 occurs before 4. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: The events \(X\) and \(Y\) are mutually exclusive

options.label: D
options.text: Event \(X\) is more likely than event \(Y\)

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
By symmetry \(P(X) = P(Y) = \frac{1}{2}\). The relative order of 1, 2 and the relative order of 3, 4 involve disjoint elements; of the 4 equally likely combinations of the two orders, exactly one has both, so \(P(X \cap Y) = \frac{1}{4} = P(X)P(Y)\). So \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.
They are not mutually exclusive (both can happen), neither must occur (2 before 1 and 4 before 3 is possible), and they are equally likely.

questions.text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

options.label: A
options.text: In the cycle stealing mode of DMA, one word of data is transferred between an I/O device and main memory in a stolen cycle

options.label: B
options.text: For bulk data transfer, the burst mode of DMA has a higher throughput than the cycle stealing mode

options.label: C
options.text: Programmed I/O mechanism has a better CPU utilization than the interrupt driven I/O mechanism

options.label: D
options.text: The CPU can start executing an interrupt service routine faster with vectored interrupts than with non-vectored interrupts

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
(A) True: cycle stealing transfers one word per stolen bus cycle.
(B) True: burst mode holds the bus for the whole block, so bulk transfer is faster.
(C) False: in programmed I/O the CPU busy-waits polling the device, wasting cycles; interrupt driven I/O frees the CPU until the device is ready, so it has better CPU utilization.
(D) True: a vectored interrupt supplies the ISR address directly, so no polling to find the source is needed.

questions.text:
A user starts browsing a webpage hosted at a remote server. The browser opens a single TCP connection to fetch the entire webpage from the server. The webpage consists of a top-level index page with multiple embedded image objects. Assume that all caches (e.g., DNS cache, browser cache) are all initially empty. The following packets leave the user's computer in some order.
(i) HTTP GET request for the index page
(ii) DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address
(iii) HTTP GET request for an image object
(iv) TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server
Which one of the following is the CORRECT chronological order (earliest in time to latest) of the packets leaving the computer ?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution: The browser first needs the server's IP address, so the DNS request (ii) goes first. Then it opens a TCP connection with SYN (iv). Over that connection it requests the index page (i), and only after parsing the index page does it know about and request the embedded images (iii). Order: (ii), (iv), (i), (iii).

questions.text: Given an integer array of size N, we want to check if the array is sorted (in either ascending or descending order). An algorithm solves this problem by making a single pass through the array and comparing each element of the array only with its adjacent elements. The worst-case time complexity of this algorithm is
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution: In the worst case (a sorted array) the single pass compares all \(N-1\) adjacent pairs, which takes \(\Theta(N)\) time. \(\Theta(N)\) means both \(O(N)\) and \(\Omega(N)\).

options.label: C
options.text: The program gets stuck in an infinite loop

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution: First iteration: \(a = 6/12 + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1\) (integer division), then \(a += 0\) gives 1. Next: \(1/12 + 1 = 1\) again. \(a\) stays 1, which is always below 10, so the loop never ends.

options.label: B
options.text: The program will terminate with no output

options.label: C
options.text: The program will terminate with 4321 as output

options.label: D
options.text: The program will terminate with 1234 as output

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution: Each call reads one character into its own local a. The calls read '1', '2', '3', '4', then the fifth call reads the newline character and does not recurse; it also prints nothing. Returning, each earlier call prints its own character after the deeper call has finished: '4', then '3', '2', '1'. Output: 4321, and the program terminates.

questions.text: Let S be the specification: "Instructors teach courses. Students register for courses. Courses are allocated classrooms. Instructors guide students." Which one of the following ER diagrams CORRECTLY represents S?
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
Entities must be Instructor, Course, Student, Classroom; relationships Teaches (Instructor, Course), Registration (Student, Course), Allocation (Course, Classroom), Guides (Instructor, Student).
(i) shows Student as a relationship (diamond) and Registration as an entity: wrong.
(ii) has no Student entity; it uses Projects: wrong.
(iii) Allocation is not connected to Classroom and Course; Classroom joins Course directly: wrong.
(iv) has every entity and relationship connected correctly.

questions.text: In a B\(^+\) tree, the requirement of at least half-full (50%) node occupancy is relaxed for which one of the following cases?
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution: Every node except the root must be at least half full. The root may hold as few as one key (two children if it is internal), so the rule is relaxed only for the root.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about a relation R in first normal form (1NF) is/are TRUE ?

options.label: A
options.text: R can have a multi-attribute key

options.label: B
options.text: R cannot have a foreign key

options.label: C
options.text: R cannot have a composite attribute

options.label: D
options.text: R cannot have more than one candidate key

questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
1NF only requires every attribute to be atomic (single-valued, not composite or multivalued).
(A) True: a key may consist of several attributes.
(B) False: foreign keys have nothing to do with 1NF.
(C) True: a composite attribute is not atomic, so a 1NF relation cannot have one.
(D) False: a relation may have several candidate keys in any normal form.

questions.text: Let \(L_1, L_2\) be two regular languages and \(L_3\) a language which is not regular. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
(A) False: \(L_1 \cap \overline{L_2} = \phi\) only says \(L_1 \subseteq L_2\). Example: \(L_1 = \phi\), \(L_2 = \Sigma^*\).
(B) False: take \(L_1 = \Sigma^*\); then \(L_1 \cup L_3 = \Sigma^*\), which is regular.
(C) True: if \(\overline{L_3}\) were regular, its complement \(L_3\) would be regular, since regular languages are closed under complement.
(D) True: complements and unions of regular languages are regular.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about threads is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Threads can only be implemented in kernel space

options.label: B
options.text: Each thread has its own file descriptor table for open files

options.label: C
options.text: All the threads belonging to a process share a common stack

options.label: D
options.text: Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
(A) False: user-level threads are implemented in a user-space library.
(B) False: the file descriptor table belongs to the process and is shared by all its threads.
(C) False: each thread has its own stack (and registers and program counter).
(D) True: threads share one address space, so one thread can read or overwrite another's data; there is no protection between them by default.

questions.text: Which of the following process state transitions is/are NOT possible?
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
(A) Possible: preemption by the scheduler or a time-slice expiry.
(B) Not possible: when the awaited event occurs a waiting process goes to Ready; it must be dispatched from Ready to run.
(C) Not possible: a process waits only by requesting I/O or an event, which it can do only while Running.
(D) Possible: the process finishes or is killed while running.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are Bottom-Up Parser(s)?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution: Shift-reduce parsers build the parse tree from the leaves up by reducing handles, and LR parsers are shift-reduce parsers: both bottom-up. Predictive and LL(1) parsers expand from the start symbol: top-down.

questions.text: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be two events in a probability space with \(P(A) = 0.3\), \(P(B) = 0.5\), and \(P(A \cap B) = 0.1\). Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: The two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent

options.label: C
options.text: \(P(A \cap B^c) = 0.2\), where \(B^c\) is the complement of the event \(B\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(P(A^c \cap B^c) = 0.4\), where \(A^c\) and \(B^c\) are the complements of the events \(A\) and \(B\), respectively

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics

questions.text: Consider the circuit shown below where the gates may have propagation delays. Assume that all signal transitions occur instantaneously and that wires have no delays. Which of the following statements about the circuit is/are CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: With no propagation delays, the output \(\mathbf{Y}\) is always logic Zero

options.label: B
options.text: With no propagation delays, the output \(\mathbf{Y}\) is always logic One

options.label: C
options.text: With propagation delays, the output \(\mathbf{Y}\) can have a transient logic One after \(\mathbf{X}\) transitions from logic Zero to logic One

options.label: D
options.text: With propagation delays, the output \(\mathbf{Y}\) can have a transient logic Zero after \(\mathbf{X}\) transitions from logic One to logic Zero

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
\(Y = X \cdot \overline{X}\).
(A) True: with no delays \(X \cdot \overline{X} = 0\) always.
(B) False, from (A).
(C) True: when \(X\) goes 0 to 1, the AND gate sees \(X = 1\) at once, but the NOT output stays 1 for one inverter delay, so both inputs are 1 briefly and \(Y\) pulses to 1.
(D) False: when \(X\) goes 1 to 0, the direct input becomes 0 at once, so \(Y\) is 0 throughout; its steady value is already 0, so there is no transient Zero.

questions.text: TCP client P successfully establishes a connection to TCP server Q. Let \(N_P\) denote the sequence number in the SYN sent from P to Q. Let \(N_Q\) denote the acknowledgement number in the SYN ACK from Q to P. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: The sequence number \(N_P\) is chosen randomly by P

options.label: B
options.text: The sequence number \(N_P\) is always 0 for a new connection

options.label: C
options.text: The acknowledgement number \(N_Q\) is equal to \(N_P\)

options.label: D
options.text: The acknowledgement number \(N_Q\) is equal to \(N_P + 1\)

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution:
(A) True: the initial sequence number is chosen (pseudo)randomly to avoid confusion with old segments and spoofing.
(B) False, from (A).
(C) False and (D) True: a SYN consumes one sequence number, so Q acknowledges the next byte it expects, \(N_P + 1\).

questions.text: Consider a 5-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB) stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction

options.label: B
options.text: In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the input of the EX stage of the next instruction

options.label: C
options.text: Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls

options.label: D
options.text: Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the pipeline stages

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
(A) True: this is the definition of forwarding (bypassing): a result is sent directly from where it is produced to the stage that needs it, without waiting for writeback.
(B) True: the value at the MEM stage output (for example a loaded word) can be forwarded to the EX input of a following dependent instruction; a load followed by a dependent instruction needs one stall and then uses exactly this path.
(C) True: a load followed immediately by an instruction that uses the loaded value still needs a one-cycle stall even with forwarding.
(D) False: forwarding needs extra multiplexers, paths and hazard detection logic.

questions.text: Which of the following fields is/are modified in the IP header of a packet going out of a network address translation (NAT) device from an internal network to an external network?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution:
(A) Modified: the private source address is replaced by the NAT device's public address.
(B) Not modified: the destination is the external host, unchanged.
(C) Modified: the header changed (source IP, and TTL is decremented), so the checksum is recomputed.
(D) Not modified: the header and payload lengths stay the same.

questions.text: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be non-empty finite sets such that there exist one-to-one and onto functions (i) from \(A\) to \(B\) and (ii) from \(A \times A\) to \(A \cup B\). The number of possible values of \(|A|\) is __________
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let \(|A| = n \geq 1\). A bijection from \(A\) to \(B\) gives \(|B| = n\). A bijection from \(A \times A\) to \(A \cup B\) gives \(|A \cup B| = n^2\). But \(n \leq |A \cup B| \leq 2n\), so \(n^2 \leq 2n\), giving \(n \leq 2\).
\(n = 1\): take \(B = A\), so \(|A \cup B| = 1 = 1^2\). Works.
\(n = 2\): take \(B\) disjoint from \(A\), so \(|A \cup B| = 4 = 2^2\). Works.
So \(|A|\) can be 1 or 2: 2 possible values.

questions.text:
Consider the operator precedence and associativity rules for the integer arithmetic operators given in the table below.

| Operator | Precedence | Associativity |
|---|---|---|
| \(+\) | Highest | Left |
| \(-\) | High | Right |
| \(*\) | Medium | Right |
| \(/\) | Low | Right |

The value of the expression \(3 + 1 + 5 * 2 / 7 + 2 - 4 - 7 - 6 / 2\) as per the above rules is __________
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
/ binds loosest, so split at the two / operators. / is right associative: the expression is \(X / (Y / 2)\) with \(X = 3 + 1 + 5 * 2\) and \(Y = 7 + 2 - 4 - 7 - 6\).
\(X\): + binds tighter than *, so \(X = (3 + 1 + 5) * 2 = 18\).
\(Y\): first the + gives \(9 - 4 - 7 - 6\); the minus operator is right associative: \(9 - (4 - (7 - 6)) = 9 - (4 - 1) = 6\).
\(Y / 2 = 3\), and \(X / 3 = 18 / 3 = 6\).

questions.text: The number of spanning trees in a complete graph of 4 vertices labelled A, B, C, and D is _________
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: By Cayley's formula a complete graph on \(n\) labelled vertices has \(n^{n-2}\) spanning trees: \(4^{2} = 16\).

questions.text:
Consider the following two relations, R(A,B) and S(A,C):

R

| A | B |
|---|---|
| 10 | 20 |
| 20 | 30 |
| 30 | 40 |
| 30 | 50 |
| 50 | 95 |

S

| A | C |
|---|---|
| 10 | 90 |
| 30 | 45 |
| 40 | 80 |

The total number of tuples obtained by evaluating the following expression
\[\sigma_{B<C}\left(R \bowtie_{R.A=S.A} S\right)\]
is _________
questions.subject: Databases
questions.chapter: Relational Algebra, Tuple Calculus and SQL
questions.solution:
Matching A values: A = 10 gives (10, 20, 90); A = 30 gives (30, 40, 45) and (30, 50, 45). A = 20 and A = 50 have no partner in S.
Apply \(B < C\): \(20 < 90\) yes, \(40 < 45\) yes, \(50 < 45\) no. So 2 tuples.

questions.text:
Consider a network path P—Q—R between nodes P and R via router Q. Node P sends a file of size \(10^6\) bytes to R via this path by splitting the file into chunks of \(10^3\) bytes each. Node P sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.
Each of the links P—Q and Q—R has a bandwidth of \(10^6\) bits/sec, and negligible propagation latency. Router Q immediately transmits every packet it receives from P to R, with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router Q can simultaneously receive on link P—Q and transmit on link Q—R.
Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time \(t = 0\).
Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which R receives all the chunks of the file?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution:
Number of chunks = \(10^6 / 10^3 = 1000\). Each chunk is 8000 bits, so it takes \(8000 / 10^6 = 0.008\) s on each link.
P puts the last chunk on the link from 7.992 s to 8.000 s. Q has the whole chunk at 8.000 s (it must receive a packet fully before forwarding it) and its earlier chunks have already left, so it sends the last chunk from 8.000 s to 8.008 s.
R has all chunks at 8.008 s.

questions.text:
Consider the following syntax-directed definition (SDD).

| Production | Semantic rule |
|---|---|
| \(S \rightarrow DHTU\) | \(\{ S.val = D.val + H.val + T.val + U.val; \}\) |
| \(D \rightarrow\) "M" \(D_1\) | \(\{ D.val = 5 + D_1.val; \}\) |
| \(D \rightarrow \epsilon\) | \(\{ D.val = -5; \}\) |
| \(H \rightarrow\) "L" \(H_1\) | \(\{ H.val = 5 * 10 + H_1.val; \}\) |
| \(H \rightarrow \epsilon\) | \(\{ H.val = -10; \}\) |
| \(T \rightarrow\) "C" \(T_1\) | \(\{ T.val = 5 * 100 + T_1.val; \}\) |
| \(T \rightarrow \epsilon\) | \(\{ T.val = -5; \}\) |
| \(U \rightarrow\) "K" | \(\{ U.val = 5; \}\) |

Given "MMLK" as the input, which one of the following options is the CORRECT value computed by the SDD (in the attribute \(S.val\))?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
"MMLK" parses as D = MM, H = L, T = \(\epsilon\), U = K.
D: innermost \(D \rightarrow \epsilon\) gives \(-5\); then \(5 + (-5) = 0\); then \(5 + 0 = 5\). So \(D.val = 5\).
H: \(H_1 \rightarrow \epsilon\) gives \(-10\); \(H.val = 50 + (-10) = 40\).
T: \(T.val = -5\). U: \(U.val = 5\).
\(S.val = 5 + 40 - 5 + 5 = 45\).

questions.text:
Consider the following grammar \(G\), with \(S\) as the start symbol. The grammar \(G\) has three incomplete productions denoted by (1), (2), and (3).
\[S \rightarrow daT \mid (1)\]
\[T \rightarrow aS \mid bT \mid (2)\]
\[R \rightarrow (3) \mid \epsilon\]
The set of terminals is \(\{a, b, c, d, f\}\). The FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the different non-terminals are as follows.
FIRST(\(S\)) = \(\{c, d, f\}\), FIRST(\(T\)) = \(\{a, b, \epsilon\}\), FIRST(\(R\)) = \(\{c, \epsilon\}\)
FOLLOW(\(S\)) = FOLLOW(\(T\)) = \(\{c, f, \$\}\), FOLLOW(\(R\)) = \(\{f\}\)
Which one of the following options CORRECTLY fills in the incomplete productions?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
FIRST(\(T\)) contains \(\epsilon\) but not \(c\), so (2) must be \(T \rightarrow \epsilon\), not \(T \rightarrow cT\). This leaves (A) and (B).
FIRST(\(S\)) must contain \(c\). With \(S \rightarrow Rf\), FIRST(\(S\)) gets \(\{c, f\}\) from \(R\) and \(f\), plus \(d\): \(\{c, d, f\}\). With \(S \rightarrow fR\) it would be only \(\{d, f\}\). So (1) is \(S \rightarrow Rf\).
Check (A): from \(S \rightarrow Rf\), FOLLOW(\(R\)) = \(\{f\}\). From \(R \rightarrow cTR\), FOLLOW(\(T\)) gets FIRST(\(R\)) minus \(\epsilon\) = \(\{c\}\) and, since \(R\) can vanish, FOLLOW(\(R\)) = \(\{f\}\). \(S \rightarrow daT\) and \(T \rightarrow aS\) make FOLLOW(\(S\)) = FOLLOW(\(T\)), which also has \$. So both are \(\{c, f, \$\}\). Everything matches.

questions.text:
Consider the following pseudo-code.
```text
L1:   t1 = -1
L2:   t2 = 0
L3:   t3 = 0
L4:   t4 = 4 * t3
L5:   t5 = 4 * t2
L6:   t6 = t5 * M
L7:   t7 = t4 + t6
L8:   t8 = a[t7]
L9:   if t8 <= max goto L11
L10:  t1 = t8
L11:  t3 = t3 + 1
L12:  if t3 < M goto L4
L13:  t2 = t2 + 1
L14:  if t2 < N goto L3
L15:  max = t1
```
Which one of the following options CORRECTLY specifies the number of basic blocks and the number of instructions in the largest basic block, respectively ?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.chapter: Code Optimisation and Data Flow Analysis
questions.solution:
Leaders: L1 (first instruction); jump targets L3, L4, L11; instructions right after a conditional jump L10, L13, L15.
Blocks: {L1, L2}, {L3}, {L4 to L9}, {L10}, {L11, L12}, {L13, L14}, {L15}.
That is 7 basic blocks, and the largest, L4 to L9, has 6 instructions.

questions.text:
Consider the following two threads T1 and T2 that update two shared variables a and b. Assume that initially a = b = 1. Though context switching between threads can happen at any time, each statement of T1 or T2 is executed atomically without interruption.

| T1 | T2 |
|---|---|
| a = a + 1; | b = 2 * b; |
| b = b + 1; | a = 2 * a; |

Which one of the following options lists all the possible combinations of values of a and b after both T1 and T2 finish execution?
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
a is changed by a = a + 1 (T1) and a = 2 * a (T2); b by b = b + 1 (T1) and b = 2 * b (T2).
Final a: if T1's step runs first, \((1+1) \times 2 = 4\); if T2's runs first, \(1 \times 2 + 1 = 3\). Final b likewise: 4 if T1's b step comes first, 3 if T2's comes first.
Order constraints: T1 does a before b, T2 does b before a. a = 3 needs T2's a step before T1's a step, so T2's b step also precedes T1's a step and hence T1's b step: b = 3. So (3, 4) is impossible.
Possible: T1 entirely first gives (4, 4); T2 entirely first gives (3, 3); any interleaving with T1's a step before T2's a step and T2's b step before T1's b step gives (4, 3), for example a = a + 1; b = 2 * b; b = b + 1; a = 2 * a.
So the set is {(4, 4), (3, 3), (4, 3)}.

questions.text: An array [82, 101, 90, 11, 111, 75, 33, 131, 44, 93] is heapified. Which one of the following options represents the first three elements in the heapified array?
questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution:
Bottom-up build of a max-heap (1-based positions, children of \(i\) are \(2i\) and \(2i+1\)):
\(i = 5\): 111 vs child 93, no change.
\(i = 4\): 11 vs 131, 44: swap with 131. Array: 82, 101, 90, 131, 111, 75, 33, 11, 44, 93.
\(i = 3\): 90 vs 75, 33, no change.
\(i = 2\): 101 vs 131, 111: swap with 131; then 101 vs 11, 44, no change. Array: 82, 131, 90, 101, 111, 75, 33, 11, 44, 93.
\(i = 1\): 82 vs 131, 90: swap with 131; 82 vs 101, 111: swap with 111; 82 vs 93: swap. Array: 131, 111, 90, 101, 93, 75, 33, 11, 44, 82.
First three: 131, 111, 90. (A min-heap would start 11, 44, 33, which is not an option.)

questions.text:
Consider the following recurrence relation:
\[T(n) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{n}\,T(\sqrt{n}) + n & \text{for } n \geq 1, \\ 1 & \text{for } n = 1. \end{cases}\]
Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution:
Divide by \(n\): \(\frac{T(n)}{n} = \frac{T(\sqrt{n})}{\sqrt{n}} + 1\). Let \(S(n) = \frac{T(n)}{n}\); then \(S(n) = S(\sqrt{n}) + 1\).
Taking square roots repeatedly reaches a constant after \(\log\log n\) steps, so \(S(n) = \Theta(\log\log n)\) and \(T(n) = \Theta(n \log\log n)\).

questions.text: Consider a binary min-heap containing 105 distinct elements. Let \(k\) be the index (in the underlying array) of the maximum element stored in the heap. The number of possible values of \(k\) is
questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution: In a min-heap every internal node is smaller than its children, so the maximum must be a leaf, and any leaf can hold it. With 105 elements (1-based) the internal nodes are 1 to \(\lfloor 105/2 \rfloor = 52\), so the leaves are positions 53 to 105: \(105 - 52 = 53\) possible values.

questions.text: The symbol \(\rightarrow\) indicates functional dependency in the context of a relational database. Which of the following options is/are TRUE?

options.label: C
options.text: \(((X, Y) \rightarrow Z\) and \(W \rightarrow Y)\) implies \((X, W) \rightarrow Z\)

questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
(A) False: the left side cannot be shrunk; \(X\) alone need not determine \(Z, W\).
(B) True: decomposition rule.
(C) True: pseudo-transitivity. From \(W \rightarrow Y\), augmentation gives \(XW \rightarrow XY\), and \(XY \rightarrow Z\), so \(XW \rightarrow Z\).
(D) True: transitivity.

questions.text: Let \(G\) be a directed graph and \(T\) a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in \(G\) that is rooted at a vertex \(v\). Suppose \(T\) is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in \(G\), rooted at \(v\). Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph \(G\) and tree \(T\) ?

options.label: A
options.text: There are no back-edges in \(G\) with respect to the tree \(T\)

options.label: B
options.text: There are no cross-edges in \(G\) with respect to the tree \(T\)

options.label: C
options.text: There are no forward-edges in \(G\) with respect to the tree \(T\)

options.label: D
options.text: The only edges in \(G\) are the edges in \(T\)

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution:
In a BFS tree every edge \(u \rightarrow w\) satisfies \(\text{depth}(w) \leq \text{depth}(u) + 1\).
(C) True: a forward edge goes from \(u\) to a proper descendant that is not its child, so to depth at least \(\text{depth}(u) + 2\). That breaks the BFS property, so none can exist.
(A) False: \(G\) with edges \(v \rightarrow u\), \(u \rightarrow v\). The tree \(v \rightarrow u\) is both the DFS and the BFS tree, and \(u \rightarrow v\) is a back edge.
(B) False: \(G\) with edges \(v \rightarrow a\), \(v \rightarrow b\), \(b \rightarrow a\). DFS visiting \(a\) first gives tree \(\{v \rightarrow a, v \rightarrow b\}\), which is also the BFS tree, and \(b \rightarrow a\) is a cross edge.
(D) False: the two examples above have edges outside \(T\).

questions.text:
Consider the following read-write schedule \(S\) over three transactions \(T_1\), \(T_2\), and \(T_3\), where the subscripts in the schedule indicate transaction IDs:
\[S: r_1(z); w_1(z); r_2(x); r_3(y); w_3(y); r_2(y); w_2(x); w_2(y);\]
Which of the following transaction schedules is/are conflict equivalent to \(S\) ?
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
Conflicting pairs: on y, \(r_3(y)\) before \(w_2(y)\), \(w_3(y)\) before \(r_2(y)\) and \(w_3(y)\) before \(w_2(y)\): all give \(T_3 \rightarrow T_2\). \(T_1\) touches only z, which no one else uses, so it has no edges. \(T_2\) and \(T_3\) do not both touch x.
A serial schedule is conflict equivalent to \(S\) exactly when \(T_3\) comes before \(T_2\); \(T_1\) can be anywhere.
(A) \(T_1T_2T_3\): \(T_2\) before \(T_3\), no. (B), (C), (D) all keep \(T_3\) before \(T_2\), yes.

questions.text:
Consider a Boolean expression given by \(F(X, Y, Z) = \sum(3, 5, 6, 7)\).
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

options.label: C
options.text: \(F(X, Y, Z)\) is independent of input \(Y\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(F(X, Y, Z)\) is independent of input \(X\)

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
Minterms 3 (011), 5 (101), 6 (110), 7 (111) are exactly the inputs with at least two 1s: the majority function.
(A) True: the maxterms are the remaining indices 0, 1, 2, 4.
(B) True: the K-map groups (3,7), (5,7), (6,7) give \(YZ + XZ + XY\).
(C) False: \(F(1,0,0) = 0\) but \(F(1,1,0) = 1\), so \(Y\) matters.
(D) False: \(F(0,1,0) = 0\) but \(F(1,1,0) = 1\), so \(X\) matters.

options.label: A
options.text: If the inputs are x=20, y=10, then the return value is greater than \(2^{20}\)

options.label: B
options.text: If the inputs are x=20, y=20, then the return value is greater than \(2^{20}\)

options.label: C
options.text: If the inputs are x=20, y=10, then the return value is less than \(2^{10}\)

options.label: D
options.text: If the inputs are x=10, y=20, then the return value is greater than \(2^{20}\)

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
Each pass of the loop does \(x \leftarrow 2x + y\), and it runs \(y\) times. Adding \(y\) to both sides, \(x + y\) doubles on every pass, so the function returns \(f(x, y) = (x + y)\cdot 2^{y} - y\).

(A) False: \(f(20, 10) = 30 \times 2^{10} - 10 = 30710\), which is less than \(2^{20} = 1048576\).

(B) True: \(f(20, 20) = 40 \times 2^{20} - 20 = 41943020 > 2^{20}\). It still fits in a 32-bit int.

(C) False: \(f(20, 10) = 30710\) is not less than \(2^{10} = 1024\).

(D) True: \(f(10, 20) = 30 \times 2^{20} - 20 = 31457260 > 2^{20}\).

So B and D.

questions.text: Let \(A\) be any \(n \times m\) matrix, where \(m > n\). Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the system of linear equations \(Ax = 0\) ?

options.label: A
options.text: There exist at least \(m - n\) linearly independent solutions to this system

options.label: B
options.text: There exist \(m - n\) linearly independent vectors such that every solution is a linear combination of these vectors

options.label: C
options.text: There exists a non-zero solution in which at least \(m - n\) variables are 0

options.label: D
options.text: There exists a solution in which at least \(n\) variables are non-zero

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
rank\((A) = r \leq n\), so the null space has dimension \(m - r \geq m - n\).
(A) True: a basis of the null space gives at least \(m - n\) independent solutions.
(B) False: if \(r < n\) the null space has dimension more than \(m - n\) and cannot be spanned by \(m - n\) vectors. Example: \(A = 0\).
(C) False: \(A = [1 \ 1]\) (\(n = 1, m = 2\)). Every non-zero solution is \((t, -t)\), with no zero entry, but \(m - n = 1\).
(D) False: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Every solution is \((0, 0, t)\), with at most 1 non-zero variable, but \(n = 2\).

questions.text:
Consider the 5-state DFA \(M\) accepting the language \(L(M) \subset (0 + 1)^*\) shown below. For any string \(w \in (0 + 1)^*\) let \(n_0(w)\) be the number of 0's in \(w\) and \(n_1(w)\) be the number of 1's in \(w\).
Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.label: D
options.text: Any string \(w\) with \(n_0(w) = n_1(w)\) is in \(L(M)\)

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
Transitions: 1: 0 to 2, 1 to 4. 2: 0 to 3, 1 to 1. 3: 0 to 1, 1 to 2. 4: 0 to 1, 1 to 5. 5: 0 to 4, 1 to 1. State 1 is the start and only final state.
A 0 adds 1 and a 1 subtracts 1 from \(n_0 - n_1\) modulo 3: state 1 means 0, states 2 and 5 mean 1, states 3 and 4 mean 2 (check: 5 on 0 goes to 4, i.e. \(1 + 1 = 2\); 4 on 1 goes to 5, i.e. \(2 - 1 = 1\)). So \(L(M) = \{w : n_0(w) - n_1(w) \equiv 0 \pmod 3\}\), and the minimal DFA merges 2 with 5 and 3 with 4.
(A) True: 2 and 4 have different residues; '1' takes 2 to the final state 1 and 4 to 5.
(B) False: 3 and 4 are equivalent.
(C) False: 2 and 5 are equivalent.
(D) True: \(n_0 = n_1\) gives difference 0.
The FALSE statements are B and C.

questions.text: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. Let \(G\) be any graph with \(n\) vertices and chromatic number \(k\). Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: \(G\) contains a complete subgraph with \(k\) vertices

options.label: B
options.text: \(G\) contains an independent set of size at least \(n/k\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(G\) contains a vertex of degree at least \(k\)

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
(A) False: there are triangle-free graphs with chromatic number 4 (for example the Grötzsch graph), so a large chromatic number does not force a large clique. Even \(C_5\) has \(k = 3\) and no triangle.
(B) True: a proper \(k\)-colouring splits the \(n\) vertices into \(k\) independent colour classes, so one has at least \(n/k\) vertices.
(C) True: in a colouring with exactly \(k\) colours that is optimal, every pair of colour classes must have an edge between them (otherwise the two classes could be merged into one colour). That is at least \(\binom{k}{2} = k(k-1)/2\) edges.
(D) False: \(K_k\) has chromatic number \(k\) but every degree is \(k - 1\).

questions.text: Consider the operators \(\Diamond\) and \(\Box\) defined by \(a \Diamond b = a + 2b\), \(a \Box b = ab\), for positive integers. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: C
options.text: Operator \(\Diamond\) over the operator \(\Box\) obeys the distributive law

options.label: D
options.text: Operator \(\Box\) over the operator \(\Diamond\) obeys the distributive law

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
(A) False: \((a \Diamond b) \Diamond c = a + 2b + 2c\) but \(a \Diamond (b \Diamond c) = a + 2b + 4c\).
(B) True: \(\Box\) is ordinary multiplication, which is associative.
(C) False: \(a \Diamond (b \Box c) = a + 2bc\) but \((a \Diamond b) \Box (a \Diamond c) = (a + 2b)(a + 2c)\); with \(a = b = c = 1\) these are 3 and 9.
(D) True: \(a \Box (b \Diamond c) = a(b + 2c) = ab + 2ac = (a \Box b) \Diamond (a \Box c)\).

questions.text: Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: WBC, which uses the write back policy, and WTC, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: A read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block

options.label: B
options.text: A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to main memory

options.label: C
options.text: A write hit in WBC can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block

options.label: D
options.text: A write miss in WTC always writes the victim cache block to main memory before loading the missed block to the cache

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
(A) False: in a write back cache the LRU victim chosen on a read miss may be dirty, and it is then evicted (written back).
(B) True: in a write through cache main memory is always up to date, so no block is ever dirty and a victim is simply overwritten.
(C) True: a write hit on a clean block sets its dirty bit from 0 to 1.
(D) False: in write through the victim is never dirty, so it never needs to be written back; the write itself goes to memory.

questions.text: Consider a 512 GB hard disk with 32 storage surfaces. There are 4096 sectors per track and each sector holds 1024 bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard disk is _________
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
One track holds \(4096 \times 1024 = 2^{22}\) bytes. One cylinder has one track on each of 32 surfaces: \(2^{5} \times 2^{22} = 2^{27}\) bytes.
Capacity \(512\) GB \(= 2^{39}\) bytes. Cylinders \(= 2^{39} / 2^{27} = 2^{12} = 4096\).

questions.text:
The baseline execution time of a program on a 2 GHz single core machine is 100 nanoseconds (ns). The code corresponding to 90% of the execution time can be fully parallelized. The overhead for using an additional core is 10 ns when running on a multicore system. Assume that all cores in the multicore system run their share of the parallelized code for an equal amount of time.
The number of cores that minimize the execution time of the program is ________
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
With \(p\) cores: serial part 10 ns, parallel part \(90/p\) ns, overhead \(10(p-1)\) ns.
\(T(p) = 10 + \frac{90}{p} + 10(p - 1)\).
\(T(1) = 100\), \(T(2) = 10 + 45 + 10 = 65\), \(T(3) = 10 + 30 + 20 = 60\), \(T(4) = 10 + 22.5 + 30 = 62.5\), and it keeps rising after that (minimum of \(\frac{90}{p} + 10p\) at \(p = 3\)).
So 3 cores minimise the time.

questions.text: A given program has 25% load/store instructions. Suppose the ideal CPI (cycles per instruction) without any memory stalls is 2. The program exhibits 2% miss rate on instruction cache and 8% miss rate on data cache. The miss penalty is 100 cycles. The speedup (rounded off to two decimal places) achieved with a perfect cache (i.e., with NO data or instruction cache misses) is _________
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
Per instruction: instruction fetch stalls \(0.02 \times 100 = 2\) cycles; data stalls \(0.25 \times 0.08 \times 100 = 2\) cycles.
Actual CPI \(= 2 + 2 + 2 = 6\). Perfect-cache CPI = 2.
Speedup \(= 6 / 2 = 3.00\).

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
Each process in the loop forks once per iteration, so the number of processes doubles each iteration, and every process (parent and child) runs printf once per iteration. wait() only orders them; each child continues the loop with its own copy of x.
Iteration with x = 3: 2 processes print. x = 2: 4 processes print. x = 1: 8 processes print.
Total \(= 2 + 4 + 8 = 14\).

questions.text:
Consider the entries shown below in the forwarding table of an IP router. Each entry consists of an IP prefix and the corresponding next hop router for packets whose destination IP address matches the prefix. The notation "/N" in a prefix indicates a subnet mask with the most significant N bits set to 1.

| Prefix | Next hop router |
|---|---|
| 10.1.1.0/24 | R1 |
| 10.1.1.128/25 | R2 |
| 10.1.1.64/26 | R3 |
| 10.1.1.192/26 | R4 |

This router forwards 20 packets each to 5 hosts. The IP addresses of the hosts are 10.1.1.16, 10.1.1.72, 10.1.1.132, 10.1.1.191, and 10.1.1.205 . The number of packets forwarded via the next hop router R2 is _______
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution:
Ranges of the last byte: /24 covers 0 to 255 (R1), /25 at 128 covers 128 to 255 (R2), /26 at 64 covers 64 to 127 (R3), /26 at 192 covers 192 to 255 (R4). Longest match wins.
16: only /24, R1. 72: /26 at 64, R3. 132: /25, R2. 191: /25 (not in 192 to 255), R2. 205: /26 at 192, R4.
R2 gets 2 hosts \(\times\) 20 packets = 40.

questions.text: Let \(G = (V, \Sigma, S, P)\) be a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with \(\Sigma = \{a, b, c\}\) and \(V\) containing 10 variable symbols including the start symbol \(S\). The string \(w = a^{30}b^{30}c^{30}\) is derivable from \(S\). The number of steps (application of rules) in the derivation \(S \rightarrow^* w\) is _________
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
In CNF, a rule \(A \rightarrow BC\) adds one variable and \(A \rightarrow a\) turns one variable into a terminal. A string of length \(n\) needs \(n - 1\) rules of the first kind and \(n\) of the second: \(2n - 1\) steps.
Here \(n = 90\), so \(2 \times 90 - 1 = 179\).

questions.text: The number of edges present in the forest generated by the DFS traversal of an undirected graph \(G\) with 100 vertices is 40. The number of connected components in \(G\) is _________
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution: The DFS forest has one tree per connected component, and a forest with \(V\) vertices and \(c\) trees has \(V - c\) edges. So \(100 - c = 40\), giving \(c = 60\).

questions.text:
Consider the following two regular expressions over the alphabet \(\{0,1\}\):
\[r = 0^* + 1^*\]
\[s = 01^* + 10^*\]
The total number of strings of length less than or equal to 5, which are neither in \(r\) nor in \(s\), is _________
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
All strings of length 0 to 5: \(1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 = 63\).
\(r\): \(\epsilon\) plus \(0^k\) and \(1^k\) for \(k = 1\) to 5: \(1 + 10 = 11\) strings.
\(s\): \(01^{k-1}\) and \(10^{k-1}\) for \(k = 1\) to 5: 10 strings. For \(k = 1\) these are '0' and '1', already in \(r\); the other 8 are not in \(r\).
\(|r \cup s| = 11 + 8 = 19\). Neither: \(63 - 19 = 44\).

questions.text: Consider a memory management system that uses a page size of 2 KB. Assume that both the physical and virtual addresses start from 0. Assume that the pages 0, 1, 2, and 3 are stored in the page frames 1, 3, 2, and 0, respectively. The physical address (in decimal format) corresponding to the virtual address 2500 (in decimal format) is _________
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
Page size 2048. \(2500 = 1 \times 2048 + 452\): page 1, offset 452.
Page 1 is in frame 3, so the physical address is \(3 \times 2048 + 452 = 6144 + 452 = 6596\).

questions.text: A bag contains 10 red balls and 15 blue balls. Two balls are drawn randomly without replacement. Given that the first ball drawn is red, the probability (rounded off to 3 decimal places) that both balls drawn are red is _________
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Given the first ball is red, both are red exactly when the second is red. 9 red remain among 24 balls: \(\frac{9}{24} = 0.375\).

questions.text:
Consider a digital logic circuit consisting of three 2-to-1 multiplexers M1, M2, and M3 as shown below. X1 and X2 are inputs of M1. X3 and X4 are inputs of M2. A, B, and C are select lines of M1, M2, and M3, respectively.
For an instance of inputs \(\mathbf{X1=1}\), \(\mathbf{X2=1}\), \(\mathbf{X3=0}\), and \(\mathbf{X4=0}\), the number of combinations of A, B, C that give the output \(\mathbf{Y=1}\) is _________
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
M1 chooses between X1 = 1 and X2 = 1, so Q1 = 1 for any A. M2 chooses between X3 = 0 and X4 = 0, so Q2 = 0 for any B.
M3 sends Q1 to Y when C = 0 and Q2 when C = 1. So Y = 1 exactly when C = 0, with A and B free: \(2 \times 2 = 4\) combinations.

questions.text: Consider sending an IP datagram of size 1420 bytes (including 20 bytes of IP header) from a sender to a receiver over a path of two links with a router between them. The first link (sender to router) has an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) size of 542 bytes, while the second link (router to receiver) has an MTU size of 360 bytes. The number of fragments that would be delivered at the receiver is ________
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution:
Payload = 1400 bytes. Fragment payloads (except the last) must be multiples of 8.
Link 1 (MTU 542): at most 522 data bytes, so 520. Fragments carry 520, 520, 360.
Link 2 (MTU 360): at most 340 data bytes, so 336. The router splits each fragment again: 520 = 336 + 184, 520 = 336 + 184, 360 = 336 + 24.
Fragments delivered: \(2 + 2 + 2 = 6\).
